findings.explanation: aws_batch_job_queue.batch has no compute_environment_order (and no service_environment_order) block. A Batch job queue with no compute environment attached cannot run any job submitted to it — jobs will sit in RUNNABLE state indefinitely. terraform validate doesn't catch this because compute_environment_order is schema-optional (to support the newer service_environment_order alternative), so this only surfaces as silent job starvation at runtime.
findings.title: Job queue has no compute environment to route jobs to

findings.explanation: compute_resources.desired_vcpus is set to a static 2, but AWS Batch actively adjusts this value at runtime in response to queue depth. Without a lifecycle.ignore_changes entry for it, every subsequent terraform plan reports drift, and an apply will forcibly reset desired_vcpus back to 2 — potentially scaling down active compute capacity mid-job. This is a well-documented gotcha with aws_batch_compute_environment.
findings.title: Compute environment doesn't ignore AWS-managed desired_vcpus drift

findings.explanation: Without a retry_strategy block, a job that fails due to a transient issue (e.g. Spot interruption, a brief dependency outage) fails permanently instead of being retried automatically.
findings.title: Job definition has no retry_strategy

findings.explanation: Without a timeout block, a job that hangs (stuck process, deadlock, waiting on an unavailable dependency) runs indefinitely, consuming compute capacity and cost with no automatic cutoff.
findings.title: Job definition has no execution timeout

findings.explanation: var.security_group_ids defaults to ["sg-05749b21616ab0cdc"] and var.subnets defaults to ["subnet-05808ec64faaa18ba"] — both look like real resource IDs from a specific AWS account/VPC, baked in as defaults on a reusable, publishable module. A consumer who forgets to override them won't get a clear error until AWS Batch's API rejects the security group/subnet as not found or not accessible to their account, rather than an obvious 'you must set this' failure at plan time.
findings.remediation: Either drop the defaults so these become required inputs (safer for a reusable module — forces every consumer to supply their own values), or clearly document in the description that the defaults are example-only IDs from the module author's own test account and must be overridden.
findings.title: Reusable module ships live, account-specific resource IDs as variable defaults

suggested_policies.rationale: aws_batch_job_queue resources are non-functional without a compute environment attached, but this is schema-optional so terraform validate never catches it. This pattern is unambiguous and fires correctly on any aws_batch_job_queue.
suggested_policies.yaml:
id: HLD_AWS_XXX  # get real ID via `holden next-id --cloud AWS`
name: Batch job queues must have at least one compute or service environment
principle: reliability
severity: MEDIUM
rationale: |
  A job queue with no compute_environment_order (and no service_environment_order)
  cannot route any submitted job to compute capacity. Jobs sit in RUNNABLE state
  indefinitely. terraform validate does not catch this because the attribute is
  schema-optional, so the gap only surfaces as silent job starvation at runtime.
message: |
  aws_batch_job_queue has no compute_environment_order and no service_environment_order — submitted jobs have nowhere to run.
remediation: |
  Add a compute_environment_order block:
    compute_environment_order {
      order               = 1
      compute_environment = aws_batch_compute_environment.example.arn
    }
resources:
  aws_batch_job_queue:
    path: compute_environment_order
    not_empty: true

suggested_policies.rationale: aws_batch_compute_environment.compute_resources.desired_vcpus is actively managed by AWS at runtime; without a matching lifecycle.ignore_changes entry, Terraform will fight AWS's own autoscaling on every plan/apply and can forcibly reset active capacity. This is a well-known, deterministic gotcha specific to this resource type/attribute pair.
suggested_policies.yaml:
id: HLD_AWS_XXX  # get real ID via `holden next-id --cloud AWS`
name: Batch compute environments should ignore AWS-managed desired_vcpus drift
principle: reliability
severity: MEDIUM
rationale: |
  AWS Batch adjusts compute_resources.desired_vcpus at runtime based on queue
  depth. Without a lifecycle.ignore_changes entry for it, every terraform plan
  reports spurious drift, and an apply can forcibly reset desired_vcpus,
  disrupting active compute capacity mid-job.
message: |
  aws_batch_compute_environment does not ignore_changes on compute_resources[0].desired_vcpus.
remediation: |
  Add a lifecycle block:
    lifecycle {
      ignore_changes = [compute_resources[0].desired_vcpus]
    }
resources:
  aws_batch_compute_environment:
    path: lifecycle.ignore_changes
    contains: "compute_resources[0].desired_vcpus"
